units.sourceHTML:
The type of SDS strings is just the char pointer ⟦CODE0⟧. However SDS defines
an ⟦CODE1⟧ type as alias of ⟦CODE2⟧ in its header file: you should use the
⟦CODE3⟧ type in order to make sure you remember that a given variable in your
program holds an SDS string and not a C string, however this is not mandatory.
units.originalInnerHTML: The type of SDS strings is just the char pointer char *. However SDS defines an sds type as alias of char * in its header file: you should use the sds type in order to make sure you remember that a given variable in your program holds an SDS string and not a C string, however this is not mandatory.

units.sourceHTML: SDS strings are created, and heap allocated, via the ⟦CODE0⟧ function, or other similar functions that we'll see in a moment.
units.originalInnerHTML: SDS strings are created, and heap allocated, via the sdsnew() function, or other similar functions that we'll see in a moment.

units.sourceHTML: SDS strings can be passed to ⟦CODE0⟧ like any other C string.
units.originalInnerHTML: SDS strings can be passed to printf() like any other C string.

units.sourceHTML: SDS strings require to be freed with ⟦CODE0⟧, since they are heap allocated.
units.originalInnerHTML: SDS strings require to be freed with sdsfree(), since they are heap allocated.

units.sourceHTML: The ⟦CODE1⟧ function is similar to ⟦CODE2⟧ but instead of creating the string assuming that the input string is null terminated, it gets an additional length parameter. This way you can create a string using binary data:⟦PRE0⟧

protected.html:
char buf[3];
sds mystring;

buf[0] = 'A';
buf[1] = 'B';
buf[2] = 'C';
mystring = sdsnewlen(buf,3);
printf("%s of len %d\n", mystring, (int) sdslen(mystring));

output> ABC of len 3

units.sourceHTML:
Note: ⟦CODE0⟧ return value is casted to ⟦CODE1⟧ because it returns a ⟦CODE2⟧
type. You can use the right ⟦CODE3⟧ specifier instead of casting.
units.originalInnerHTML: Note: sdslen return value is casted to int because it returns a size_t type. You can use the right printf specifier instead of casting.

units.sourceHTML:
The ⟦CODE1⟧ function creates an empty zero-length string:

⟦PRE0⟧
units.originalInnerHTML:
The sdsempty() function creates an empty zero-length string:

sds mystring = sdsempty();
printf("%d\n", (int) sdslen(mystring));

output> 0

units.sourceHTML:
The ⟦CODE1⟧ function duplicates an already existing SDS string:

⟦PRE0⟧
units.originalInnerHTML:
The sdsdup() function duplicates an already existing SDS string:

sds s1, s2;

s1 = sdsnew("Hello");
s2 = sdsdup(s1);
printf("%s %s\n", s1, s2);

output> Hello Hello

protected.html:
sds s1, s2;

s1 = sdsnew("Hello");
s2 = sdsdup(s1);
printf("%s %s\n", s1, s2);

output> Hello Hello

units.sourceHTML: Obtaining the string length
units.originalInnerHTML: Obtaining the string length

units.sourceHTML: It runs in constant time since the length is stored in the prefix of SDS strings, so calling ⟦CODE0⟧ is not expensive even when called with very large strings.
units.originalInnerHTML: It runs in constant time since the length is stored in the prefix of SDS strings, so calling sdslen is not expensive even when called with very large strings.

units.sourceHTML: The function is binary safe like any other SDS string function, so the length is the true length of the string regardless of the content, there is no problem if the string includes null term characters in the middle.
units.originalInnerHTML: The function is binary safe like any other SDS string function, so the length is the true length of the string regardless of the content, there is no problem if the string includes null term characters in the middle.

units.sourceHTML: Destroying strings
units.originalInnerHTML: Destroying strings

units.sourceHTML:
The destroy an SDS string there is just to call ⟦CODE0⟧ with the string
pointer. However note that empty strings created with ⟦CODE1⟧ need to be
destroyed as well otherwise they'll result into a memory leak.
units.originalInnerHTML: The destroy an SDS string there is just to call sdsfree with the string pointer. However note that empty strings created with sdsempty need to be destroyed as well otherwise they'll result into a memory leak.

units.sourceHTML:

units.sourceHTML: Concatenating strings
units.originalInnerHTML: Concatenating strings

units.sourceHTML:
Concatenating strings to other strings is likely the operation you will end
using the most with a dynamic C string library. SDS provides different
functions to concatenate strings to existing strings.
units.originalInnerHTML:
Concatenating strings to other strings is likely the operation you will end
using the most with a dynamic C string library. SDS provides different
functions to concatenate strings to existing strings.

units.sourceHTML:
The main string concatenation functions are ⟦CODE0⟧ and ⟦CODE1⟧ that are
identical, the only difference being that ⟦CODE2⟧ does not have an explicit
length argument since it expects a null terminated string.
units.originalInnerHTML: The main string concatenation functions are sdscatlen and sdscat that are identical, the only difference being that sdscat does not have an explicit length argument since it expects a null terminated string.
